fields.verificationNote: No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Checked here: Theorem 1.1 was read against Lech's question as the paper states it from Lech (1960, 1964); it claims $e(R)\le e(S)$ for every flat local homomorphism of nonzero Noetherian local rings, with no restriction on dimension, residue fields or characteristic. The proof was not refereed. It uses the perfectoid normalized lengths of Cai-Lee-Ma-Schwede-Tucker in mixed characteristic and Eisenbud-Schreyer vector bundles. The family's Lean challenge (DuttaDomain, found via lean/docs/194.md, not in formalization.yaml) states only a supporting characteristic-$p$ comparison over complete local domains, not Lech's inequality, so this entry is left Unreviewed; that statement is entered separately.
fields.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for every flat local homomorphism $(R,\mathfrak m)\to(S,\mathfrak n)$ of nonzero Noetherian local rings, $e(R)\le e(S)$, in all dimensions and characteristics. The key input is a uniform lower bound on the zeroth homology of finite free complexes with entries in high powers of a parameter ideal, valid for generalized length functions, applied with Frobenius perfection in characteristic $p$ and perfectoid lengths in mixed characteristic. The paper does not claim the stronger Iyengar-Ma-Walker conjecture for all complete local rings, only its complete-domain characteristic-$p$ case.

fields.name: The Iyengar-Ma-Walker Dutta multiplicity conjecture for complete local domains of positive characteristic
fields.field: Commutative algebra; Dutta multiplicity of short complexes
fields.statement: Over a $d$-dimensional Noetherian local ring $R$, a short complex is a finite free complex in degrees $0,\dots,d$ with finite-length homology and nonzero zeroth homology. In characteristic $p>0$ its Dutta multiplicity is $\chi_\infty(F)=\lim_n p^{-nd}\sum_i(-1)^i\ell(H_i(\Phi^nF))$, where $\Phi^n$ raises differential entries to $p^n$-th powers. Iyengar, Ma and Walker (2022, Conjecture 8.1) conjectured $\chi_\infty(F)\ge e(R)$ for short complexes over complete local rings, which would imply Lech's conjecture (their Proposition 8.3). For every complete Noetherian local domain of characteristic $p>0$ and every short complex $F$, is $\chi_\infty(F)\ge e(R)$?
fields.posedBy: Srikanth B. Iyengar, Linquan Ma and Mark E. Walker, Multiplicities and Betti numbers in local algebra via lim Ulrich points, Algebra & Number Theory 16 (2022), Conjecture 8.1

fields.name: The Kervaire conjecture: adjoining one generator and one relator never kills a nontrivial group
fields.field: Combinatorial group theory; equations over groups
fields.statement: Let $A$ be a nontrivial group, let $t$ generate an infinite cyclic group, and let $w$ be any element of the free product $A*\langle t\rangle$. Kervaire's characterization of high-dimensional knot groups (1965) led to the group-theoretic question whether the quotient $(A*\langle t\rangle)/\langle\langle w\rangle\rangle$ can ever be trivial, that is, whether $A*\mathbb Z$ can be normally generated by one element. Known cases included torsion-free $A$ (Klyachko, unimodular case), residually finite and hyperlinear $A$ (via Gerstenhaber-Rothaus and Pestov), and $w$ of special forms. Is $(A*\langle t\rangle)/\langle\langle w\rangle\rangle$ nontrivial for every nontrivial group $A$ and every $w$?
fields.posedBy: Michel Kervaire, Les noeuds de dimensions superieures (1965); the group-theoretic form is traced to this setting by Chen (2026)
fields.ageNote: The manuscript cites Kervaire (1965) for the knot-group origin and Chen's survey for the group-theoretic formulation. The stronger Kervaire-Laudenbach injectivity form is covered by the separate entry for Howie's conjecture.
fields.aiRole: The release README says the manuscripts were produced by an unreleased internal OpenAI model, the vast majority by one fixed procedure using on average about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute per result, and that some outputs build on earlier results produced by the models. Its named exceptions to that procedure (the zeta zero-free region work, whose Re(s) > 11/12 write-up was human edited, and the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties) do not concern this family. Both manuscripts of the family are credited to OpenAI with no human author named. The Kervaire manuscript proves the result directly through a spectral-phase inequality in the group von Neumann algebra and a fixed-space theorem for unitary matrices; the later nonsingular-systems manuscript (5 October 2026) names it as its direct antecedent.
fields.verificationNote: No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 of the principal manuscript were read against the conjecture as posed: Corollary 1.2 is the nontriviality statement for every nontrivial $A$ and every word $w$. The Lean challenge ComparatorChallenges/Kervaire.json (theorem OAI.Kervaire.coefficient_injective, solution module OAI.GroupTheory.Kervaire.Main, present at the pinned commit) is not in the formalization catalogue formalization.yaml; it was found through lean/docs/256.md. Its statement was read here: for every group $A$ and every $w$ in the coproduct of $A$ with multiplicative $\mathbb Z$ whose exponent sum is $\pm1$, the map from $A$ to the quotient by the normal closure of $w$ is injective. That is Theorem 1.1, which is stronger than the headline for unimodular words; the remaining exponent sums follow by the one-line surjection onto $\mathbb Z/d$ given in the paper, which is not itself formalised. Permitted axioms are propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice. Not rebuilt here. The manuscript records that Kawauchi (2024) published a proposed resolution through ribbon sphere-link groups, which it does not use.
fields.resultNote: Claims Theorem 1.1: for every group $A$ (no torsion, cardinality or presentation hypothesis) and every $w\in A*\langle t\rangle$ with exponent sum $\pm1$ in $t$, the canonical map $A\to(A*\langle t\rangle)/\langle\langle w\rangle\rangle$ is injective, so the equation $w(t)=1$ is solvable in an overgroup. Corollary 1.2: the quotient is nontrivial for every $w$ when $A\ne1$, which is the Kervaire conjecture. It does NOT prove injectivity for other nonzero exponent sums (the Kervaire-Laudenbach form); that is the companion's nonsingular-systems theorem. It does not assert a solution inside $A$ itself.

fields.name: Howie's conjecture: every nonsingular system of equations over a group is solvable in an overgroup
fields.field: Combinatorial group theory; equations over groups
fields.statement: Let $G$ be a group and $w_1,\dots,w_m\in G*F(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ a system of equations $w_i=1$ with coefficients in $G$. Its exponent-sum matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb Z)$ records the exponent of each $x_j$ in each $w_i$; the system is nonsingular if $A$ has rank $m$ over $\mathbb Q$. Gerstenhaber and Rothaus (1962) solved nonsingular systems over finite groups and compact Lie groups, Howie (1981) over locally indicable groups, and Nitsche-Thom over hyperlinear groups. The one-equation, one-variable case is the Kervaire-Laudenbach conjecture (a nonzero exponent sum should guarantee solvability). Does every finite nonsingular system over an arbitrary group $G$ have a solution in some group containing $G$, that is, is $G\to(G*F_n)/\langle\langle w_1,\dots,w_m\rangle\rangle$ injective?
fields.posedBy: James Howie (1981), On pairs of 2-complexes and systems of equations over groups; name and formulation as in Klyachko, Mikheenko and Roman'kov (2024)
fields.ageNote: The manuscript takes the name and formulation from Klyachko, Mikheenko and Roman'kov (2024, Introduction) and cites Howie (1981) for the locally indicable case; 1981 is used as the posing year on that basis. Its one-variable case, the Kervaire-Laudenbach conjecture, goes back to the Kervaire problem of 1965.

The manuscript is credited to OpenAI with no human author named. It states that its spectral-phase and planar-surface strategy comes from the family's earlier Kervaire manuscript (24 September 2026), extended by a multi-block fixed-space theorem for products of unitary groups.

fields.name: Khot's 2-to-1 Games Conjecture with perfect completeness
fields.field: Hardness of approximation; PCPs and label cover
fields.statement: A 2-to-1 game is a bipartite projection game with left alphabet $[2q]$ and right alphabet $[q]$ in which every constraint map has exactly two preimages of each right label (Khot's original formulation allowed fibers of size at most two). Its value is the largest fraction of constraints satisfied by one labeling. Khot (2002) conjectured that for every $\delta>0$ there is a fixed alphabet size for which it is NP-hard to distinguish satisfiable 2-to-1 games from games of value at most $\delta$. Khot, Minzer and Safra (2018) proved the version with completeness $1-\varepsilon$; perfect completeness, which is what several coloring and satisfiable-CSP reductions need, was known only with soundness about $23/24$ (Austrin-O'Donnell-Tan-Wright), and Fei-Minzer-Wang had it for 4-to-1 games. Is it NP-hard, for every fixed $\delta>0$, to distinguish satisfiable 2-to-1 games from those of value at most $\delta$?

fields.ageNote: Khot's original statement allows fibers of size at most two; the manuscript proves the exact-two version, which implies it.

fields.name: The Auslander-Reiten conjecture for Artin algebras
fields.field: Representation theory of algebras; homological conjectures
fields.statement: Let $R$ be an Artin algebra (for example a finite-dimensional algebra over a field) and $M$ a finitely generated $R$-module. Auslander and Reiten (1975), in their work on the generalized Nakayama conjecture, conjectured that $M$ must be projective if $\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(M,M\oplus R)=0$ for every $i>0$. It was proved for many classes (complete intersections, radical cube zero, Igusa-Todorov algebras, rings satisfying Auslander's condition), and Schulz's non-projective module without self-extensions lives over a skew field, outside this setting. The Gorenstein-projective conjecture (Luo-Huang) is its restriction to Gorenstein-projective modules. Is every finitely generated module $M$ over an Artin algebra with $\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(M,M\oplus R)=0$ for all $i>0$ projective?

fields.name: The Nakayama conjecture on dominant dimension
fields.field: Representation theory of algebras; homological conjectures
fields.statement: Let $\Lambda$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field with minimal injective resolution $0\to\Lambda\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots$. Must a finite-dimensional algebra of infinite dominant dimension be self-injective?

fields.name: The local p-adic section conjecture for curves of genus at least two
fields.field: Anabelian geometry; etale fundamental groups of p-adic curves
fields.statement: Let $k$ be a finite extension of $\mathbb Q_p$ and $X/k$ a smooth proper geometrically connected curve of genus at least two, with arithmetic etale fundamental group sequence $1\to\pi_1(X_{\bar k})\to\pi_1(X)\to G_k\to1$. The local p-adic section conjecture, the local analogue of the section conjecture in Grothendieck's 1983 letter to Faltings, asserts that this map from $X(k)$ to conjugacy classes of sections is a bijection. Is every section of $\pi_1(X)\to G_k$ induced by a unique rational point of $X$?

fields.name: A uniform bound of three on generalized star height (the generalized star-height problem)
fields.shortName: Generalized star height at most three
fields.field: Automata and formal languages; regular expressions
fields.statement: A generalized regular expression over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ is built from $0$, $1$ and letters by union, concatenation, complement in $\Sigma^*$ and Kleene star; its height is the nesting depth of stars, and $h(L)$ is the least height of an expression for a regular language $L$. With complement, height zero is exactly the star-free languages (Schutzenberger), height at most one was known for languages recognized by abelian groups, nilpotent groups of class two and some semigroups (Pin-Straubing-Therien, Bourne-Ruskuc), and no language of generalized height above one is known. Straubing distinguishes two questions: does one height bound serve for all regular languages, and does height one always suffice? Is there a uniform bound on generalized star height, and is it one?

fields.name: The finitely presented Burnside problem: is every finitely presented periodic group finite?
fields.field: Group theory; Burnside-type finiteness problems
fields.statement: A group is periodic if every element has finite order. Burnside (1902) asked how such conditions constrain finitely generated groups. Golod (1964) built infinite finitely generated periodic groups, Novikov and Adian infinite groups of bounded exponent, and Grigorchuk an infinite finitely generated 2-group, but none of these is finitely presented, and Ol'shanskii-Sapir's finitely presented torsion-by-cyclic groups have an infinite cyclic quotient. The finite-presentation version of Burnside's question asks whether a group given by finitely many generators and finitely many relators (in the ordinary sense, not within a variety) can be infinite while every element has finite order. Is every finitely presented periodic group finite?

fields.name: Must a finitely presented nil algebra be nilpotent? (Ufnarovskij's question)
fields.field: Noncommutative ring theory; nil and radical algebras

fields.name: Pointwise convergence of multiple ergodic averages for mixing transformations
fields.field: Ergodic theory; multiple ergodic averages
fields.statement: Let $T$ be an invertible measure-preserving transformation of a probability space and $f_1,\dots,f_n$ bounded measurable functions. Since Furstenberg's ergodic proof of Szemeredi's theorem, the multiple ergodic averages $\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^N\prod_{j=1}^n f_j(T^{jk}x)$ have been central. Host-Kra and Ziegler proved convergence in $L^2$ for every $n$, but almost-everywhere convergence was known only for $n=2$ (Bourgain) and under extra structure for larger $n$: K-systems, weakly mixing systems with spectral or joining restrictions, and distal systems (Huang-Shao-Ye). The general pointwise question asks whether these averages converge almost everywhere for every $n$ and every system; it was open even for mixing $T$. Do the multiple ergodic averages converge almost everywhere for every finite length?

fields.name: The Courtade-Kumar conjecture: dictators are the most informative Boolean functions
fields.field: Boolean functions; information theory
fields.statement: Let $X$ be uniform on $\{0,1\}^n$ and let $Y$ be $X$ passed through independent binary symmetric channels with crossover probability $\varepsilon\in[0,1/2]$. Kumar and Courtade (2013, 2014) conjectured that for every Boolean function $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$, $I(f(X);Y)\le1-h_2(\varepsilon)$ bits, the value attained by a dictator $f(x)=x_i$. Partial results covered high-noise ranges (Ordentlich-Shayevitz-Weinstein, Samorodnitsky, Yu), balanced functions in ranges, and coordinatewise sums (Courtade-Kumar; Javanmard-Woodruff). Does every Boolean function satisfy $I(f(X);Y)\le1-h_2(\varepsilon)$ for every $n$ and every $\varepsilon$?
fields.posedBy: Gowtham R. Kumar and Thomas A. Courtade, Which Boolean functions are most informative? (ISIT 2013); Courtade and Kumar (IEEE Trans. IT 2014)

Both manuscripts of the family are credited to OpenAI with no human author named. fields.name: The Hellinger conjecture for Boolean functions under product noise
fields.field: Boolean functions; information theory
fields.statement: Let $X$ be uniform on $\{-1,1\}^n$, let $T_\rho$ be the noise operator with correlation $\rho\in[-1,1]$, and write $H(t)=\sqrt{1-t^2}$. Anantharam, Bogdanov, Chakrabarti, Jayram and Nair (2017) conjectured that for every Boolean $f$ with mean $m$, $H(m)-\mathbb E\,H(T_\rho f)\le1-\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$, with equality for dictators: a single coordinate maximizes the loss of Hellinger affinity. They showed it implies the Courtade-Kumar conjecture. Known results included a Gaussian-isoperimetric lower bound (Chen-Nair) and the sharp balanced low-noise consequence (Durcik-Ivanisvili-Roos-Xie). Does the Hellinger inequality hold for every Boolean function, of any bias, and every $\rho$?
fields.posedBy: Venkat Anantharam, Andrej Bogdanov, Amit Chakrabarti, T. S. Jayram and Chandra Nair (ITA Workshop manuscript, February 2017)

The manuscript is credited to OpenAI with no human author named. fields.name: The Lane-Emden conjecture for elliptic systems, with its Henon-weighted extension
fields.field: Elliptic systems; Liouville theorems
fields.statement: The Lane-Emden system is $-\Delta u=v^p$, $-\Delta v=u^q$ in $\mathbb R^n$ with $p,q>0$. The Lane-Emden conjecture asserts that it has no positive classical entire solution in the subcritical region $\frac1{p+1}+\frac1{q+1}>\frac{n-2}n$, with no symmetry or decay assumption. It was proved for $n\le2$, for $n=3$ (Serrin-Zou; Polacik-Quittner-Souplet) and $n=4$ (Souplet), and in partial ranges for $n\ge5$. Phan (2012, Conjecture C) posed the weighted Henon-Lane-Emden form $-\Delta u=|x|^Av^p$, $-\Delta v=|x|^Bu^q$ for $A,B>-2$, with subcritical region $\frac{n+A}{p+1}+\frac{n+B}{q+1}>n-2$, and Huang and Zou stated it for all real weights with solutions continuous at the origin. Is there no positive entire solution throughout the subcritical region, in every dimension?
fields.posedBy: Lane-Emden conjecture: Liouville literature of the 1990s (Mitidieri 1993, 1996; Serrin and Zou 1996); weighted form: Phan (2012), Conjecture C; Huang and Zou (2026), Conjecture B
fields.ageNote: The manuscript cites Mitidieri (1993, 1996), Serrin-Zou (1996) and Souplet's 'proof of the Lane-Emden conjecture in four space dimensions' (2009) but does not say who first stated the unweighted conjecture; Phan's weighted Conjecture C dates from 2012 (arXiv 2011).
fields.aiRole: The release README says the manuscripts were produced by an unreleased internal OpenAI model, the vast majority by one fixed procedure using on average about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute per result, and that some outputs build on earlier results produced by the models. Its named exceptions to that procedure (the zeta zero-free region work, whose Re(s) > 11/12 write-up was human edited, and the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties) do not concern this family. The manuscript is credited to OpenAI with no human author named. It combines a localized potential-kernel virial identity with an energy-relative interval-pressure estimate; the radial existence theorem of Bidaut-Veron and Giacomini used for the classification is credited to them.
fields.verificationNote: No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 were read against the conjecture: for $n\ge2$, $p,q>0$, real $A,B$ in the weighted subcritical region, no positive solutions continuous on $\mathbb R^n$ and $C^2$ off the origin; the unweighted Lane-Emden conjecture is the case $A=B=0$, $n\ge3$. formalization.yaml lists ComparatorChallenges/HenonEmden.json, declaration OAI.HenonLaneEmden.main_nonexistence, file OAI/Analysis/HenonEmden/Main.lean. The statement was read here: for $n\ge2$, $p,q>0$, real $A,B$ with $(n+A)/(p+1)+(n+B)/(q+1)>n-2$, there are no $u,v$ on Euclidean $n$-space that are continuous, $C^2$ off the origin, strictly positive and satisfy both equations away from the origin. That is the headline nonexistence claim. The existence half of Phan's Conjecture C (via the cited radial theorem) is not formalised. Permitted axioms are propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice. Not rebuilt here.
fields.resultNote: Claims Theorem 1.1: for every $n\ge2$, $p,q>0$ and $A,B\in\mathbb R$ with $\frac{n+A}{p+1}+\frac{n+B}{q+1}>n-2$, the Henon-Lane-Emden system has no positive solution continuous at the origin and $C^2$ elsewhere, with no condition at infinity. Corollary 1.2 is the unweighted Lane-Emden conjecture; with Bidaut-Veron and Giacomini's radial existence theorem this gives Phan's Conjecture C in full for $n\ge3$, $A,B>-2$, and Huang-Zou's Conjecture B. It does NOT classify solutions on the critical hyperbola beyond the cited radial existence, and treats only positive (not sign-changing) solutions.

fields.name: Kurosh's problem for division rings: are algebraic division rings locally finite?
fields.field: Noncommutative ring theory; division algebras
fields.statement: A division ring $D$ with center $F$ is algebraic over $F$ if every element satisfies a nonzero polynomial over $F$, and locally finite if every finite subset generates a division subring of finite dimension over $F$. In 1941, in connection with Burnside's problem, Kurosh asked whether a division ring that is algebraic and finitely generated as an algebra over a central subfield must be finite-dimensional over it. Golod's nil algebras answer the analogous question for general algebras but contain nilpotents, so they do not touch division rings; Jacobson and Kaplansky settled the bounded-degree and polynomial-identity cases. Is every division ring that is algebraic over its center locally finite?
fields.posedBy: A. G. Kurosh, Ringtheoretische Probleme, die mit dem Burnsideschen Problem uber periodische Gruppen in Zusammenhang stehen (1941), Problem (K)
fields.aiRole: The release README says the manuscripts were produced by an unreleased internal OpenAI model, the vast majority by one fixed procedure using on average about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute per result, and that some outputs build on earlier results produced by the models. Its named exceptions to that procedure (the zeta zero-free region work, whose Re(s) > 11/12 write-up was human edited, and the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties) do not concern this family. The manuscript is credited to OpenAI with no human author named. The construction is a countable inductive scheme using symbol and cyclic algebras, formal series in two noncommuting variables and a lifting theorem that makes each scheduled element algebraic.
fields.verificationNote: No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Theorem 1.1 was read against Kurosh's Problem (K): a countable division ring of characteristic zero, algebraic over its center $F$, with $D=F[x,y]$ for two elements and $[D:F]=\infty$. Since $F$ is central, this is a negative answer to the problem as Kurosh posed it (over a central subfield). No Lean formalisation exists for this family. The release README warns that some unformalised results could have issues.
fields.resultNote: Claims Theorem 1.1: there is a countable division ring $D$ of characteristic zero with center $F$ and $x,y\in D$ such that $D=F[x,y]=F(x,y)$, $[D:F]=\infty$, and every element of $D$ is algebraic over $F$ (with no uniform degree bound). So algebraicity over the center does not imply local finiteness. It does NOT give an example in positive characteristic or over a prescribed center, and polynomial degrees grow without bound, as they must by Jacobson's theorem.
